title: Mona Lisa
summary: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci. Considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance, it has been described as "the best known, the most visited, the most written about, the most sung about, [and] the most parodied work of art in the world". The painting's novel qualities include the subject's enigmatic expression, the monumentality of the composition, the subtle modelling of forms, and the atmospheric illusionism.

sections.name: her figure
sections.description: Lisa Gherardini is depicted in a three-quarter view, a pose that was revolutionary for the time. Her seated figure is monumental, filling the frame and drawing the viewer's immediate focus.

sections.name: her eyes
sections.description: Leonardo used the sfumato technique to blur the edges around her eyes, making her gaze appear soft and lifelike. This creates the illusion that her eyes follow the viewer across the room.

sections.name: her enigmatic smile
sections.description: The subtle shading at the corners of her mouth makes her expression ambiguous. It is called 'enigmatic' because it seems to shift between amusement and solemnity depending on the viewer's focus.

sections.name: the winding path and bridge
sections.description: In the mid-ground, a winding road appears on the left and a stone bridge on the right. These details ground the portrait in a physical space and provide a sense of human scale within the vast landscape.

sections.name: the misty mountains
sections.description: The distant, jagged mountains fade into a hazy blue, a technique known as aerial perspective. This creates a feeling of infinite depth and adds to the overall sense of mystery in the painting.

guide_notes.her figure: This is her whole figure: a round head at the top with two eyes and a mouth, then her shoulders and body widening below. The painting is small, about 77 by 53 centimetres, and it is painted on a thin poplar panel, not canvas.
guide_notes.her eyes: The two short lines across the top mark her brow, with an eye below each one and the line of her nose running down between them. In the painting itself she has no clear eyebrows or eyelashes, and scholars still argue whether Leonardo left them out or they were lost in an old cleaning.
guide_notes.her enigmatic smile: Near the top is the tip of her nose; below it, the curve that turns up at both ends is her smile, and the lower curve is her chin. Research by Margaret Livingstone found the smile shows up most when you look away from her mouth, because its shadowed corners are seen best from the corner of the eye.
guide_notes.the winding path and bridge: At the bottom right, the short upright bars are the arches of a stone bridge, and the lines winding above and to the left are the road. A Tuscan historian has identified it as the Romito di Laterina bridge over the Arno, in the province of Arezzo.
guide_notes.the misty mountains: Along the top are small jagged peaks, and below them a larger peak rises to a point. Leonardo made the far mountains hazy and bluish so they seem to fall away into the distance, a technique called aerial perspective.

museum_facts: The Louvre identifies the sitter as Lisa Gherardini, wife of Florentine silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo; her name gives the painting its Italian title, La Gioconda.
Leonardo used sfumato, layering glazes to create soft, smoky contours. The sitter’s turn toward the viewer adds a sense of natural movement.
The painting is on a poplar-wood panel, not canvas. The panel has warped and developed a crack, so the Louvre displays it in a temperature- and humidity-controlled glass case.
King François I invited Leonardo to France and bought the painting from him in 1518, bringing it into the royal collection.
The painting was stolen from the Louvre on 21 August 1911 and recovered more than two years later after former Louvre glazier Vincenzo Peruggia tried to sell it to an Italian art dealer.
